name: Henry VIII of England
summary: An absolute-minded Tudor monarch whose recorded positions centre on royal and national sovereignty: he broke with Rome, made himself supreme head of the English church, and enforced doctrinal conformity and loyalty by treason law and execution. His written record is mostly statutes and one late speech urging charity in religious dispute, so economic and social questions are largely unaddressed.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Preserved hereditary royal succession and governed through nobles rather than abolishing inherited rank.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The Six Articles Act of 1539, passed on his personal doctrinal intervention, made denial of transubstantiation punishable by burning and other denials of its articles felony.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: He told the Lincolnshire rebels in 1536 that the subsidy was granted him by the nobles and commons by act of parliament and not set forth by councillors on their own will, and refused to release the Fifteenth.

church-by-bishops.rationale: He told the Lincolnshire rebels it was not for them to find fault with their prince in electing his councillors and prelates, keeping the appointment of bishops with the crown.

clerical-rule.rationale: The Act of Supremacy placed the clergy beneath the crown, giving the king supreme headship of the Church of England with power to correct its errors and heresies.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: His colonial project used conquered farmland and resources to extend English royal control and reward English settlers.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Grounded subjects’ obligatory allegiance in divine command and nature, rejecting their claim to control government.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The Buggery Act 1533 made buggery with mankind or beast a felony punishable by death and forfeiture, without benefit of clergy; the text does not define the term.

death-penalty.rationale: Capital punishment for treason and heresy was routine, including burning and hanging under the Six Articles and Treasons Act.

decide-locally.rationale: He centralised power by abolishing the marcher lordships in the Laws in Wales Acts and bringing the church under one national system in the Act of Supremacy.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Explicitly required Scottish kings to recognize English superiority through homage and fealty.

democracy-best.rationale: Declared ordinary commoners unqualified to choose councillors or direct the affairs reserved to their prince.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Successive acts settled the crown by heredity; Supremacy Act annexes headship to the crown for his heirs and successors.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: He told the Lincolnshire rebels that they were bound to obey their king both by God's commandment and the law of nature.

dynastic-succession.rationale: His will of 1546 sets the succession on his son Edward and then his daughters in turn.

elective-rulers.rationale: His will of 1546 settles the succession on his children in turn, and he told the Lincolnshire rebels that commoners may not choose the prince's councillors.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Used attainder by Parliament instead of trial against Cromwell and others, and broke the pardon given to the Pilgrimage of Grace rebels.

filial-duty.rationale: Commandment V requires lifelong parental respect and material support.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Took personal command at Boulogne in 1544, built a permanent navy, and appointed and dismissed his own ministers such as Cromwell.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The King's Book of 1543, which he endorsed, bases the commandments on scripture, but he also governed through royal and parliamentary law; mixed.

majority-settlement.rationale: Personally wanted an ethnically English colony in conquered territory, populated by English farmers and soldiers.

military-superiority.rationale: He founded a permanent royal navy, building the Deptford and Woolwich dockyards and expanding the fleet from a handful of ships to dozens.

more-religion-public.rationale: Prescribed uniform Christian instruction and conduct under royal supervision.

national-church-status.rationale: Created the Church of England under the crown and enforced its doctrine by statute (Six Articles, King's Book).

national-self-determination.rationale: Claimed English sovereignty over Scotland through hereditary right and homage, rather than Scottish national choice.

natural-rulers.rationale: Distinguished the prince and selected nobles’ capacity to rule from commoners’ alleged incapacity; not a biological theory.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Commandment VI expressly permits lawful self-defense and public punishment.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Personally drove religious-conformity legislation, extending government beyond defense, justice and property protection.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: He told the Lincolnshire rebels that they were bound to obey their king by God's commandment and the law of nature, whatever their grievances.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Commandment VIII requires owners to aid needy neighbours.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Parliament enacted the Act of Supremacy but the Act vests supreme headship of the church in the king and his successors, not in Parliament.

population-transfer.rationale: Pursued an English colony through displacement of the native French population and restrictions on return.

premarital-sex.rationale: Commandment VII condemns fornication and sexual infidelity.

property-fundamental.rationale: In 1536 he told the Lincolnshire rebels that the suppression of religious houses and monasteries had been granted him by the nobles spiritual and temporal and the commons by act of parliament, defending the Crown's taking of monastic property.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Faith explicitly subordinates natural reason to religious knowledge.

refugee-return.rationale: Barred displaced inhabitants’ return to lands claimed by conquest, prioritizing English settlement in the Boulonnais.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: He fixed one official doctrine by statute with severe penalties (Six Articles Act 1539, King's Book 1543).

religious-nation.rationale: The Act of Supremacy declared him supreme head of the Church of England, one body with the realm, and the Six Articles Act enforced a single doctrine on all subjects by penalty.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: He told the Lincolnshire rebels that they were bound to obey their king and for no worldly cause to withstand their prince.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The Six Articles Act made abandoning the doctrine it set out a capital offence, while the Act of Supremacy bound subjects to the new royal headship; the penalties fell on those leaving the established settlement, though not framed as a ban on conversion.

return-lost-territory.rationale: He invaded France in 1544, took Boulogne and planned settlement, in a campaign Murphy describes as aimed at recovering lands the English crown claimed.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The Act of Supremacy made him supreme head of the Church of England, but nothing in it claims divine descent or divinity; mixed.

separate-church-state.rationale: Made himself and his successors the only supreme head of the Church of England, with power to reform doctrine and correct errors, annexed to the crown.

separated-powers.rationale: Creed and Commandment VI deny independent authorities above kings.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: He claimed plenary power and used attainders, yet acted through Parliament for the great changes; contested.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Provided publicly endowed masses, preaching and charitable support alongside his own explicitly spiritual account of human destiny.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Personally expanded royal shipbuilding through new dockyards, supply facilities and naval administration.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Acts of Appeals and Supremacy put the clergy under crown authority, and the Suppression Acts dissolved the monasteries and took their property.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The Treasons Act 1534 criminalised words against the supremacy, and he executed More, Fisher and the Pilgrimage of Grace leaders despite a promised pardon.

taxation-theft.rationale: Defended parliamentary subsidies and first-fruits as legitimate contributions subjects owed toward government and defense.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Invaded France in 1512 and 1544 seeking to recover territory, took Boulogne, and attacked Scotland; also annexed Wales and became King of Ireland in 1542.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: The King's Book (Commandment V) exempts commands contrary to God from obedience, but he told the rebels of 1536 that they must obey for no worldly cause to withstand their prince; mixed.

notes:
Religious views changed: he defended papal authority and the sacraments in the Assertio Septem Sacramentorum (1521, not read in full here), then broke with Rome in 1533-34 while keeping traditional doctrine in the Six Articles and King's Book. Answers use his mature position. Full texts of the Six Articles act, Ten Articles, King's Book and Letters and Papers were not retrieved; those are described through reference summaries.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 27 answers taken from it, 24 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent pass: previous answers were not consulted. Whole active list and remaining nulls reviewed. The 1543 doctrinal book was collaboratively prepared, personally revised and explicitly endorsed by Henry; individual sections are cited without claiming he authored every sentence. Mature religion is distinguished from his earlier papal allegiance. Six Articles evidence includes the preamble’s specific account of his personal intervention, not royal assent alone. Ordinary statutes concerning Wales, Irish clothing, sodomy, poor relief, usury or prices are not automatically attributed to him. Economic searches included a full monetary-history article and the accessible scholarly extract and references on food-price proclamations; government action without personal involvement is insufficient. Sovereign coin debasement does not itself answer modern public-versus-private bank-credit creation, deficit stimulus or central-bank independence. Moral usury language is insufficient for a current blanket interest prohibition, particularly given the later 1545 statute. Threats and exemplary execution orders are attributed to him; the historians explicitly doubt whether every order was implemented. Beaton plotting concerns extralegal assassination, not ordinary state warfare; the identity of an intermediary and the connection of earlier plots to the final killing remain disputed. Colonial officers’ independent abuses are distinguished from Henry’s policy: attacks on departing Boulogne civilians violated his initial safe-conduct orders. The later settlement program nevertheless explicitly sought an ethnically English colony; the follow-up historian attributes this aim to Henry personally. A colonial ethnic-settlement policy does not by itself establish that all nations must consist mainly of one ethnic group. Black court musician John Blanke’s employment and wedding gifts do not establish Henry’s general position on racial equality or interracial marriage. No biological racial theory, class theory of history, third-way economics or view that competition drives progress was found. The legendary Brutus genealogy supports a royal territorial claim, but is not automatically a modern doctrine of national identity. Religious conformity does not itself define national membership by religion. Sacramental theology does not establish literal interpretation of every scriptural passage. Views on slavery, modern technology, climate and universal healthcare are not invented from Tudor institutions. The portrait commission was for a restricted palace audience and does not alone demonstrate a public mass leader cult. Naval construction is strategic state investment, not proof that all major industries should be publicly owned. Only rationales starting Inferred: are historical inferences. Later pass 2026-11-13 (rules 7): sources tagged by kind and evidence; eleven answers that rested only on Wikipedia are re-sourced to the Lincolnshire reply, the Six Articles Act, the Act of Supremacy, Royal Museums Greenwich, Murphy (2016) and the text of the Buggery Act (statutes.org.uk), or nulled (the two Wales language answers: the Act's own text did not open). The one Gutenberg text by him (love letters to Anne Boleyn) is declined.
